entries.title: Bulls coming up with a plan for Dailyn Swain and it involves G League
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE – It definitely wasn’t how Dailyn Swain imagined watching his first NBA game as a member of the Bulls.</p><p>“I watched it on TV,” Swain said on Friday. “It was just tough not being there. It’s definitely weird to watch the team you play for on TV in a different city.”</p><p>Illness kept the rookie back in Chicago for that opening-season beating at the hands of the Raptors, but he was able to rejoin the team in Milwaukee and finally get his first ever NBA experience, albeit on the bench.</p><p>There is a plan in place for the No. 15 overall pick, however.</p><p>Well, sort of.</p><p>As long as the current rotation stays relatively healthy, Swain will see a lot of his early-season minutes in the G League once that tips off in a few weeks.</p><p>“It’s hard to map right now because you never know who is going to be available, who is not, but yeah, we plan to have him play in the G League, plenty of minutes, getting reps at different positions,” coach Tiago Splitter said.</p><p>Not that it’s much of a surprise for Swain. He was forced into a primary ball-handling role in Summer League and struggled, and then with Tre Jones on the shelf at the start of the preseason, again Swain saw the back-up point guard spot with mixed results.</p><p>“Now in the G league, when he goes there, I think you gotta try everything,” Splitter said. “But it is true that when you’re the first ball-handler, you make more decisions, and I think you develop more. Now, his future, his position in the NBA, I think he’s a very versatile player, he can play in different positions – on the ball, off the ball – and this is how we see him.”</p><p>As far as how Swain sees himself? Whatever it takes to get better.</p><p>“Anything to help me develop, that’s a positive thing,” he said of going to the G League. “Anything that helps my growth, I’m OK with that.”</p><p></p><p><b>Nothing to see here</b></p><p></p><p>Splitter knows that guard Josh Giddey has been dealing with a left wrist issue but didn’t deem it anything serious or to be concerned about.</p><p>Giddey told reporters that he injured the wrist early in the preseason and had been working through it. He didn’t miss preseason time or show up on the injury report, so it couldn’t have been that serious. A point Splitter confirmed.</p><p>“I’m not seeing it affect his play,” Splitter said. “I understand that he’s got something on his wrist, but I don’t think he’s having any issues playing basketball there.”</p><p></p><p><b>Early impressions</b></p><p></p><p>Of all the younger bench guys on the roster, it sounds like Splitter might already have a favorite in big Tobe Awaka.</p><p>The fact that Awaka – a two-way contract player – was one of the few bright spots in the loss in Toronto with six offensive rebounds, didn’t go unnoticed.</p><p>“I love it,” Splitter said of the rookie from Arizona. “He plays hard, he competes every possession. He goes to the board. He’s just a soldier, and he’s going to have chances. I wish everybody would bring the same spirit that he does.”</p><p></p><p><b>Boys of summer</b></p><p></p><p>Despite the Bucks having a game in Philadelphia on Saturday night, rather than flying out right after the game against the Bulls – the standard for all NBA teams – Milwaukee’s front office allowed the players to go and attend Game 1 of the World Series between the Brewers and Rays at American Family Field at 7 p.m.</p><p>The team charter was scheduled to then leave later that night, well after the baseball game.</p>

entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson shows he's far from the usual rookie in clutch win
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE – It’s not the usual type of talk from a 20-year-old rookie in the NBA.</p><p>Then again, who said Caleb Wilson was usual?</p><p>He wasn’t usual in knocking down four free throws in crunch time to help ice the Bulls’ 132-125 win over Milwaukee on Friday. He wasn’t usual in then grabbing a huge defensive rebound, and a possession later nabbing a steal on a Tyler Herro pass.</p><p>Usual talk? No, not for Wilson. He’s proving to be walking to the beat of his own drum and making sure opposing teams understand exactly who is conducting that music.</p><p>“I always feel like near the end of the game I’m going to do the right thing, and I love those moments because it shows who you really are,” Wilson said of the victory. “The thing for me is just proving myself right, like if I want to be the guy I’ve got to show up and make free throws, do clutch things in the final minutes, so just having the opportunity to do that is big.”</p><p>Especially since 19 of his 21 points came in the second half.</p><p>“I feel like in the first half I didn’t get the ball as much,” Wilson said very matter-of-factly. “One thing about the NBA is the games are long. You might not touch it in the first half but once I get my chance I’m going to go out there and do what I can. And that’s all I did. It’s a long game, your teammates have to find you, and honestly, I’m one of the focal points of our team defensively, most teams focus on me. So just having that patience and knowing it’s eventually going to come.”</p><p>That it did, as his 21 points, six rebounds, two blocks and one steal were somewhat historic as the follow up to his 15 points, one block and one steal in his debut on Wednesday. Wilson joined Michael Jordan as the only rookies in Bulls history and ninth in NBA history to have stat lines with those minimums within his first two games.</p><p>“He’s fearless, he’s a competitor, he’s a winner at the end of the day,” veteran Tre Jones said of Wilson’s efforts against Milwaukee. “He does whatever the team asks of him, he does things that the team doesn’t even ask from him, and at the end of the day he’s trying to make winning plays down the stretch and he did that.”</p><p>So did Jones, however, as coach Tiago Splitter showed his hand a bit, closing the game with the hot hands rather than the usual starting five.</p><p>Considering the embarrassment suffered in the blowout in Toronto on Wednesday, it was all hands-on deck in Splitter’s mind.</p><p>“Nobody liked the way we played,” Splitter said of that opener. “We know that, the players know that. I think we hit bottom there and it was bad.”</p><p>It was up to Splitter to make sure Game 2 of the season wasn’t, as he watched his starting unit again start off slowly, before the likes of Jones, Leonard Miller, Isaac Okoro and Buddy Hield helped right the ship.</p><p>Hield scored a quick seven points in just over four minutes of work in the second quarter, while Miller and Okoro combined for 18 points and were both a plus-12 in plus/minus.</p><p>That second group would again be called on in the fourth, as the Bulls (1-1) held a two-point lead with 8:45 left.</p><p>Come closing time it was Smith, Jones, Okoro, Norman Powell and of course Wilson, as he rode in the white horse to finish it.</p><p>“I expected to make the free throws, I expected to get the win,” Wilson added. “So nothing I didn’t expect.”</p>

entries.title: City inspects funeral home where 55 decaying bodies were found amid calls for its demolition
entries.summary: <p>As the Chicago Department of Buildings conducted an inspection Friday morning at the South Side funeral home where 55 decomposing bodies were found in August, activists and a family impacted by the discovery called for the building's demolition. </p><p>"This is a house of horrors we're standing next to," said Lisette Guillen, a crisis responder with Case Files Chicago. "The way families feel — the way most of Chicago and the surrounding areas feel — is it probably should be knocked down." </p><p>The inspection comes over two months after authorities <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" >ordered the building shut down</a> after the decaying bodies were found by police acting on a tip. </p><p>Guillen cited a number of hazards both for impacted families and the immediate surrounding community to justify demolishing the building. </p><p>"There's children that are here. There's pets that walk on the grass and take things back inside the home," Guillen said. "We don't know what the area around may have been exposed to." </p><p>Over six months after her mother Shawnese Shannon <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/28/sisters-mothers-cremated-remains-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home" target="_blank" >died from advanced cancer</a>, Marshawna Campbell and her family are still left with questions and uncertainty. </p><p>When Campbell learned that the man who had picked up her mother’s body from hospice had been accused of mishandling human remains, she and her sister opened their mother's urn and began to question everything after finding cremated remains that looked like chunks of white substance.</p><p>"All of our questions are still unanswered," Campbell told reporters outside the funeral home Friday morning. "We couldn't even celebrate my mama being gone for six months because we don't know if it's her in the urn." </p><p>A lack of information from police has left Campbell frustrated, and her voice cracked as she questioned how Clark and Johanna Morgan, the owners of the funeral home, allowed the conditions.</p><p>"What if it was you in our shoes?" Campbell said. "All y'all did was burn her skin and break her bones. I could've done that myself." </p><p></p><p></p><p>Inspectors were inside the building for over 30 minutes and came out around 10:45 a.m. without speaking, and the city's Department of Buildings, which dispatched the inspectors, did not respond to a request for comment about what they saw or whether there was any communication with the Morgans.</p><p>Also at the site of the inspection was Ald. Peter Chico (10th) and an SUV believed to be registered to Clark Morgan, though it could not be confirmed whether he or his wife were there. </p><p>Chico also did not respond to a request for comment about the inspection. </p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>The Department of Buildings said in a statement that inspectors from the department’s electrical, new construction, plumbing and demolition bureaus were at Friday's inspection, and that they will present findings in court on Oct. 29 during a hearing.</p><p>“The Department of Buildings recognizes the deep pain the families are experiencing, and our thoughts remain with them as this process moves forward. Today’s inspection was conducted pursuant to a court order requiring the Department to conduct a comprehensive inspection of the building,” the department said. <br></p>

entries.title: Canadiens much further along in their rebuild than Blackhawks are in theirs
entries.summary: <p>Five seasons ago, the Canadiens had the worst record in the NHL. But their point total has increased in every season since, including 15-point jumps in the last two seasons. They had 106 points last season and reached the conference finals.</p><p>Now that’s a rebuild.</p><p>The Blackhawks, meanwhile, had the sixth-worst record in 2021-22, then finished in the bottom three for four consecutive seasons. Their 72 points last season were 20 more than they had in 2023-24 but still were the second-fewest in the league.</p><p>That’s a much slower rebuild.</p><p>The Original Six rivals met Friday at the United Center, with the Hawks hoping — expecting, really — to catch the Habs in the rebuild race. Though his team is far behind, coach Jeff Blashill looks at the Canadiens and sees the Hawks’ future.</p><p>“Montreal was very young last year, and once it clicked, it clicked,” Blashill said. “And there’s zero doubt in my mind that once it clicks here, it’s going to really click.”</p><p>The teams are taking similar tacks in their rebuilds. Both are assembling young cores — they’re among the five youngest teams in the league — and have them under contract for several years. The Canadiens, in particular, have banded together, signing team-friendly deals to keep their core intact.</p><p>The Hawks have begun that process, but they’re still a ways from determining exactly who is in their core. Though they’re off to a slow start, Blashill thinks the talent is there.</p><p>“We have a lot of real high-end talent that just has to learn how to manage games, learn how to not beat themselves,” he said. “You’re going to figure it out at some point when you have that kind of high talent with great character, which I’m sure is what Montreal has.”</p><p>That’s the rub for the Hawks: Learning on the job.</p><p>“We beat ourselves too much,” Blashill said. “And there’s no getting around the growth process of that. We’re trying to help expedite it, but it’s still just part of it.”</p><h3>Mangiapane activated</h3><p>The Hawks activated left wing Andrew Mangiapane from injured reserve after he returned to practice in the morning skate. He suffered a lower-body injury in the season opener Sept. 29, the second consecutive opener in which Mangiapane got hurt. Last year with the Oilers, he suffered a groin injury that he played with all season.</p><p>“That’s one of the reasons why you want to make it heal, because last year I didn’t,” Mangiapane said after taking a few moments to catch his breath as he builds his stamina back up. “I think I played every game with a bum groin. You just don’t want it to be the same thing.”</p><p>Mangiapane’s status initially was day-to-day, but he said the injury lingered and he didn’t want to risk making it worse.</p><p>“Feeling good and just happy to be back and skating with the guys,” he said. “Just being in on the jokes and seeing everybody is an uplifting feeling.”</p><p>But Mangiapane isn’t guaranteed a permanent spot in the lineup.</p><p>“I think a number of guys have done a good job since he’s gone out, especially as of late,” Blashill said. “It will be a competition, for sure.”</p><p>• Defenseman Bowen Byram (upper body) returned to the ice, skating individually before practice, but he isn’t close to playing.</p><h3>Tech trouble</h3><p>Blashill has embraced players’ use of iPads on the bench, though some players who predate the technology criticize its use because players watch the game less.</p><p>“It’s a great tool to be able to get instant feedback,” Blashill said. “I wish the damn things would work more. I used to throw my controller, too, when I used to play video games. That’s probably more on me.”</p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker doling out big bucks to help Democrats — and boost a 2028 presidential run
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is pouring millions into some of the country’s most consequential midterm races that could determine just how much President Donald Trump can accomplish in his final two years in office — efforts that will also help the governor in a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/pritzker-for-president-handicapping-the-illinois-governors-political-future" > potential 2028 presidential bid.</a></p><p>Pritzker, the billionaire heir to the Hyatt empire, is not only doling out his vast personal wealth to boost candidates in contentious races. He’s also building coalitions with Democrats across the country, including in 2028 early primary states. Beyond his own political future, a Democratic-led House or Senate would be essential for any Democratic presidential candidate to get things done in the next term.</p><p>Since 2025, Pritzker has given at least $40 million to Democrats and allied causes — including campaigns for Congress, Senate, attorney general, secretary of state, county judges, and state parties in more than a dozen states, as well as ballot fights over abortion rights and redistricting. That figure includes $15 million he contributed to his own PAC called Ready for the Fight, which is running ads in Tennessee, Arkansas, Alabama and Ohio. </p><p>"He's doing everything right. I have never met him, but he is on my list of presidential candidates. So far, in the running is [Kentucky Gov. Andy] Beshear, Pritzker, and [Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] AOC in that order," said Howard Dean, former Vermont governor, presidential candidate and chair of the DNC. "I'm impressed. More more importantly than all the giving is how he's conducted his governorship. Despite my liking AOC, I'm determined, with that exception, to elect somebody who's been a governor who's not from Washington, and he fits the bill."</p><p>Dean called Pritzker's widespread Democratic contributions "investments," saying "they're not just out of the goodness of his heart."</p><p>"It's a terrific strategy," Dean said.</p><h3>Contributions spread across the country </h3><p>Pritzker kicked off his midterm campaigning for other candidates in August, attending a get-out-the-vote canvass in Orlando with Rep. Maxwell Frost and Florida gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. He has also headlined state party dinners in Oklahoma, Texas, Georgia, Indiana, Colorado, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Arizona and Texas. And since last year, he's attended fundraisers and events in South Carolina, Washington, D.C., New York, Florida, New Hampshire, Louisiana, North Carolina, Massachusetts, Nevada, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maine, Alabama, California and New Mexico.</p><p>During a NAACP conference in South Carolina last month, Pritzker described November as "an election that will define America's next chapter.</p><p>"I'm here right now because everything we care about is under siege, and I want to be where the freedom fighters are right here," Pritzker said. "And I'm here because we're in a generational battle to preserve voting rights, and that battle is on behalf of all of the people in the Palmetto State, in the land of Lincoln, my home state, and everywhere that the embers of democracy still burn bright."</p><p>Pritzker’s largest contributions this cycle include $1.5 million to the Wisconsin Democratic Party, $1.2 million to Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor, $1 million each to the Democratic Governors Association, Senate Majority PAC, Ohio Democratic Party, the House Majority PAC and Project Battleground, a leadership committee helping Keisha Lance Bottoms' Georgia gubernatorial campaign. He also gave $310,000 to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.</p><p>State party contributions include $500,000 each to the Iowa and Michigan Democratic parties, $270,000 to the Democratic Party of New Hampshire, $150,000 to the North Carolina Democratic Party, $125,000 to the Democratic Party of Georgia, $100,000 each to the Maine, South Carolina and Texas Democratic parties. South Carolina are New Hampshire are early primary states in 2028.</p><p>Senate candidate contributions include $54,300 to Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina, $50,000 to support Minnesota Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan, $7,000 each for his running mate Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton's Senate campaign, Mary Peltola's Senate campaign in Alaska, Cooper in North Carolina and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown in Ohio. He also gave $3,500 each to Kentucky Senate candidate Charles Booker, Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, New Hampshire Senate candidate Chris Pappas and <a class="Link" Pritzker wants his contributions to actually move the needle forward. entries.summary: <p>Trailing by 11 points in the second quarter and with its top running back injured, Naperville Central had a big challenge.</p><p>But the Redhawks also had Mark Williams.</p><p>The speedy junior broke free for a pair of long touchdown catches, and Naperville Central held on for an 18-14 home victory Friday against Warren in the opening round of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" >Class 8A playoffs</a>.</p><p>Williams, who was just named the DuPage Valley Conference offensive player of the year, caught four passes for 175 yards. His touchdowns came on consecutive possessions in the third quarter — a 67-yarder down the right sideline and a 74-yarder down the left sideline — and gave the Redhawks (6-4) an 18-14 lead with 1:59 left in the period.</p><p>Both passes were thrown by senior quarterback Simon Hayes, who was 12-for-24 for 254 yards.</p><p>‘‘Me and Simon have been working all summer, waiting for a moment like this,’’ Williams said. ‘‘And it just proves how good of a team we are. Our chemistry, it’s showcased with all the summer work we put in.’’</p><p>Naperville Central is heading to Oswego (8-1) for a first-round game next week a year after missing the playoffs for the first time since 2019.</p><p>‘‘I knew in the offseason we definitely had to make changes,’’ Hayes said. ‘‘Two-and-seven [last season] isn’t what Naperville Central is known for, and I think me and Mark — that kind of had a chip on our shoulder.’’</p><p>The Redhawks also have a running back with big-play capability in Ryan Jacobson. But he left with an injury after running twice for 43 yards.</p><p>‘‘I trust everyone on this team to do their job,’’ Hayes said. ‘‘And it shows. When someone goes down, the next person’s ready. And they’re going to do the best job they can.’’</p><p>Another person who stepped up was junior cornerback Eron Kennedy.</p><p>His pass breakup forced a turnover on downs at Naperville Central’s 7-yard line with 8:18 left, then he intercepted a pass with 4:17 to play.</p><p>‘‘The story of our season is how much better our defense has gotten since Week 3,’’<br>Redhawks coach Mike Ulreich said. ‘‘We went out to Prospect and played a bad football game [a 45-14 loss]. And we needed to grow up a lot and get some things corrected. . . .</p><p>‘‘And it helps that Mark Williams plays defense now. And Eron Kennedy is an unbelievable football player. At the end of the game, if they want to go at Eron with the game on the line — all day.’’</p><p>Junior Jonathan Randolph ran 24 times for 189 yards and both Blue Devils touchdowns, including a 39-yarder. He left the game late in the third quarter and didn’t return.</p><p>‘‘Johnny’s one of our great backs we’ve had around Warren for a long time,’’ coach Bryan McNulty said. ‘‘But he was showing signs of a concussion, and, like I told him on the bench, he needs that brain for another 60, 70 years.</p><p>‘‘So I’m more concerned with that. And I’m glad our trainers and everybody made the right decision to pull him out of the game.’’</p><p>Another impact player for Warren was junior Amari Conley, who stepped in at running back and rushed for 31 yards and also had two sacks on defense.</p><p>The future looks bright for the Blue Devils (4-6), who graduate only seven seniors.‘‘We should be OK,’’ McNulty said. ‘‘We need to have a good offseason, though.’’</p>

entries.title: Lane's defense dominates with 5 interceptions, 3 TDs in playoff win against Joliet Central
entries.summary: <p>Paiden Buckner, a three-year starter for Lane, did his job well this season. But the senior cornerback went through the entire regular season without an interception—the ultimate highlight moment for a player in the secondary.</p><p>Buckner picked off two passes in the Champions’ 56-0 win over Joliet Central in a Class 8A opening round playoff game Friday at Lane Stadium.</p><p>“I was surprised they even threw my way,” Buckner said. “Teams don’t usually do that. It was great, honestly; that was the best defensive game we have played this season.”</p><p>Lane’s defense dominated, holding the Steelmen to fewer than 70 total yards and picking off five interceptions.</p><p>“We knew they were a running team,” Champions coach Deshon Conley said. “I felt good if they were forced to pass the ball. I told my guys that. Let’s stop the run early and force them to pass, and we will be in good shape.”</p><p>Lane quarterback Blake Perkins punched in a one-yard touchdown on the opening drive, and junior Shamar Pipes ripped off a 59-yard touchdown run early in the second quarter to put the Champions (7-3) ahead 14-0. Pipes carried the ball eight times for 115 yards.</p><p>“I saw good blocks, and I knew there was one man I had to make a move on and go score for my team,” Pipes said. “I just have to come out and play hard for my team. They are looking for me to be a playmaker, so that’s what I went out to do.”</p><p>Perkins rushed for another touchdown late in the first half and connected with Aidan Andrich on a 24-yard touchdown late in the third quarter. entries.title: Sophomore Jaydin Edmondson is at the top of the state
entries.summary: <p>Even Comer sophomore Jaydin Edmondson is a little surprised when he checks his stats online.</p><p>At the top of the list for interceptions by Illinois players are Edmondson and Wauconda senior Luke Sickmeir, both with eight in nine games. Even if all schools around the state don’t report stats, it’s an impressive achievement.</p><p>‘‘At first I was kind of like, ‘OK, I’m doing high numbers,’ ’’ Edmondson told the Sun-Times. ‘‘But then when I start looking at MaxPreps and seeing the rankings . . . I was like, ‘Oh, this is real. I really have eight interceptions. That’s a lot.’ ’’</p><p>It hasn’t come as a surprise to Catamounts coach DeMarien Hampton, though.</p><p>‘‘He’s lined up at corner, he’s lined up at free safety, nickel,’’ Hampton told the Sun-Times. ‘‘He’s just lined up all over the field, and he just has a good sense for the football.’’</p><p>Comer, a charter school in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood, has an affiliated middle school. That’s where Edmondson first crossed Hampton’s radar.</p><p>By then, Edmondson was already an experienced player, having started as an 8-year-old with the Chicago Bengals. He always has been a two-way player at defensive back and wide receiver. This season, he’s also the top pass-catcher for Comer (5-4) with 30 receptions for 478 yards and nine touchdowns.</p><p>‘‘I love playing both ways,’’ Edmondson said. ‘‘I’ve been playing both ways since youth football.’’</p><p>He’s a big reason the Catamounts are in the state playoffs for the first time since 2022. They host Prairie Ridge (2-7) in the Class 5A opening round at 11:30 a.m. Saturday at Eckersall.</p><p>Comer enters the postseason on a five-game winning streak after an 0-4 start. This is the second program Hampton has taken to the playoffs after guiding Bowen to its only IHSA berth in 2015. He also served as an assistant at city power Morgan Park for five seasons before taking over two years ago at Comer, where he works as a dean.</p><p>One philosophy that has carried over from his Morgan Park days is playing a strong nonconference schedule. The Catamounts opened with losses to Goode, Curie, Ag. Science and Corliss. All have qualified for the playoffs with winning records, with Corliss (Red South) and Ag. Science (Red Southwest) winning conference titles.</p><p>‘‘They’re young, and that youth showed up in Week 1 [a 73-48 loss to Goode],’’ Hampton said of his players.</p><p>But the Catamounts started playing cleaner football around midseason, which Hampton expected would happen.</p><p>‘‘The football IQ is there,’’ he said.</p><p>It also helps that many of the players came up through the middle school flag program, which runs the same offense and defense as the high school.</p><p>‘‘The first thing I wanted to do when I got here was keep our good, quality guys in-house,’’ Hampton said.</p><p>Edmondson is among that group, and he’s glad he stuck around.</p><p>‘‘This is a big moment,’’ he said. ‘‘We [are] all taking it in, but we all know we have to win this game. We have to treat it like a championship game.’’</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams kept making major strides in fundamentals in sparkling performance to beat Patriots
entries.summary: <p>This is what the leap from fun quarterback to franchise quarterback looks like.</p><p>Caleb Williams has reenergized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ offense and been checking key boxes along the way. He has done it by blending his high-end talent with the foundation coach Ben Johnson laid out for him.</p><p>His fundamentals lagged in his first two seasons even as he made stunning plays, but he’s now taking steps toward being a finished product. Williams showed great timing, throwing accuracy, pocket patience and decision-making while rolling up big numbers in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-inactives-vs-patriots-lb-t-j-edwards-out-with-hamstring-injury" >the 30-24 win over the Patriots on Thursday</a> — and that performance wasn’t an outlier.</p><p>Imagine the reaction a year ago if he’d completed 22 of 33 passes for 308 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions for a 116.7 passer rating. Now it’s becoming relatively normal.</p><p>He has completed 71% of his passes this season, second in the NFL. He’s piling up easy yardage on safe, short throws. He’s leading his receivers into space. It’s the merging of electricity and efficiency that Johnson demanded.</p><p>“He has gone through the progressions a little bit quicker,” Johnson said Friday. “He's got that clock going in his head, understanding where the breakdowns are happening in protection.”</p><p>Williams has always had good pocket awareness, but not always great judgment. He needed a tough grader like Johnson to help him sharpen that, and that’s why after a 2025 season in which he made some of the most incredible plays in the league, he sat Williams down in the offseason to scrutinize over 100 incomplete passes.</p><p>Johnson’s relentlessness is one of the best parts of his approach to the job, and is a major factor in why Williams has a chance to be a championship-caliber quarterback. Johnson’s reaction to Thursday was that Williams did a ton right, but also could fix quite a bit.</p><p>“It's a great stat line, and yet I can't wait to sit down with him and go through this [snap-by-snap] because … there's still a lot more out there for us,” he said.</p><p>That’s a chore for another time.</p><p>Williams deserves credit for the work he’s done to become a more polished passer. He made plays against the Patriots that were not only vital in that game, but promising for his future.</p><p>All four passes to speedster Luther Burden were right where they needed to be as Burden went for 130 yards and a touchdown in the first half.</p><p>On Williams’ 58- and 26-yard completions, each pass was a “runner’s ball,” as he’s been calling it under Johnson, meaning Burden could catch them in stride with room to run. The Patriots didn’t allow the Bears those opportunities on the other two passes, but Williams was on target to Burden for 37 and 24 yards.</p><p>He made three crucial passes in the fourth quarter in which pressure was closing in on him and he showed great discipline by staying in the pocket and delivering the ball downfield:</p><p>- Patriots linebacker Christian Elliss got a hand on his left shoulder when he dropped back on third-and-11 from his own 13-yard line, but rather than run, Williams shook him off, held his ground and fired to Rome Odunze for 21 yards.</p><p>- Later that drive, facing fourth-and-two near midfield, Williams hung in the pocket as pressure pushed toward him from three directions and found tight end Colston Loveland for nine yards.</p><p>- His most important pass was on the Bears’ final drive as they tried to ice the game. On third-and-nine at his own 10-yard line, Williams dropped all the back to the end zone to buy time, then stepped forward a yard and sent a dart to Odunze for 21 yards.</p><p>None of those three passes produced enduring highlights, but they were solid, professional plays that led to victory. The Bears have been desperate for years to find that in a quarterback.</p>

entries.title: Is the Magnificent Mile's long-awaited revival here?
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s top shopping destination is experiencing a long-promised renaissance, following a tumultuous decade of store closures, empty storefronts and little foot traffic.</p><p>The mile-long stretch of North Michigan Avenue known as the Magnificent Mile is seeing a flurry of new store openings such as Uniqlo and the Hello Kitty Cafe, while at least five retailers have announced plans to open locations in the coming months.</p><p>“I think we are getting ready to go to our prom,” Magnificent Mile Association President Kimberly Bares said. “We're on the cusp of some of the best years that Michigan Avenue has seen."</p><p>A number of leasing deals coupled with more than $250 million in capital investments by landlords and retailer confidence pushed North Michigan Avenue’s retail vacancy down to 25.8% from 33.8% in 2025, according to October data from Chicago-based brokerage firm Kirsch Agency.</p><p>This year, American Eagle Outfitters said its returning to the Mag Mile next summer with a 14,182-square-foot flagship at 600 N. Michigan Ave. Last month, activewear brand Lululemon signed a deal to add another store at the base of the Tribune Tower, 435 N. Michigan, where they'll join incoming tenants Big City Optical and Intuit TurboTax. And the 60,000-square-foot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/04/09/candy-hall-fame-experience-museum-mag-mile" >Candy Hall of Fame Experience</a> will also open summer 2027 at 830 N. Michigan, spotlighting candy brands, innovators and confectionery history, as well as a store.</p><p>Garage, a trendy Canadian fast fashion brand, plans to open this fall at 625 N. Michigan, according to the Magnificent Mile Association. Fellow Gen Z brand Edikted is also close to finalizing a deal on the Mag Mile, according to<b> </b>brokers with knowledge of the deal. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ed0000" name="image-ed0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7880cf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F19%2F0987385c4e969f54a0530eba5439%2Fmagmile-261025-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/05bed8d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F19%2F0987385c4e969f54a0530eba5439%2Fmagmile-261025-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a59e3d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F19%2F0987385c4e969f54a0530eba5439%2Fmagmile-261025-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Japanese apparel brand Uniqlo opened a flagship store at 600 N. Nike will downsize from its 57,000-square-foot flagship into a two-level 43,000-square-foot space at the Shops at North Bridge.</p><p>The Shops at North Bridge announced in August a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/10/shops-north-bridge-river-north-40-million-makeover" >$40 million renovation</a> for the mall's interior and exterior to be completed by next year, with hopes to entice experiential retailers. It follows the $170 million redevelopment plan at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/27/metlife-170-million-water-tower-place-transformation" target="_blank" >Water Tower Place</a>, announced in April, that would transform the struggling mall's lower floors and bring in women’s specialty stores, apparel and beauty brands and experiential concepts.</p><p>“We're watching a very, very fast recovery,” Greg Kirsch, managing broker of Kirsch Agency, said. “It's not that the rents are low. It's that the sales performance is high because when they were really at their lowest, there was still no deal activity.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ec0000" name="html-embed-module-ec0000"></a><div style="min-height:610px" id="datawrapper-vis-dHbkd"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dHbkd/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-dHbkd"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dHbkd/full.png" alt="New and upcoming businesses on the Mag Mile (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3>From closings to openings</h3><p>Former Mayor Rahm Emanuel's record <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/9/3/18455831/emanuel-record-property-tax-hike-tough-but-necessary" >$500 million property tax increase</a> in 2015 impacted retailers' desire to move into prime real estate in the city because the hikes would be passed on to tenants, Kirsch said.</p><p>The Mag Mile's retail vacancy rate was a low 3.6% in 2016, but by 2018, it jumped to 12%, according to Kirsch Agency data.</p><p>“I think people forget that even before the pandemic, Michigan Avenue — because of its reliance on in-person shopping — was experiencing competition from online retailers,” Bares said.</p><p>By 2019, major retailers like Forever 21, Crate & Barrel, Best Buy, Apple and Topshop shuttered their expansive Mag Mile stores. And the following year, the pandemic brought <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2020/8/10/21362016/chicago-looting-downtown-mag-mile-shooting-lightfoot-police" >looting and an increase in violent crime</a> that lingered for years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0a0000" name="image-0a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/93bbf2b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d771ec8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9f44aa4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Shop windows at Timberland, 625 N. Michigan Ave., were shattered in 2020 after looting broke out overnight in the Loop and surrounding neighborhoods." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9f44aa4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e36ebe5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9f44aa4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5937x3332+0+191/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fa1%2F8967910b4271ab7c37a0a3813533%2Flooting-081120-10.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Shop windows at Timberland, 625 N. Michigan Ave., were shattered in 2020 after looting broke out overnight in the Loop and surrounding neighborhoods.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“One of the things that's very important in retail is that the customers feel comfortable in the environment, and when people don't feel comfortable shopping, they feel nervous or threatened or unsafe,” Kirsch said.</p><p>He said the "biggest blow" was when Macy’s closed its Water Tower Place store in 2021. The department store had been there for 45 years and accounted for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2021/1/5/22215598/macys-closing-water-tower-place-retail-department-store" >20% of the mall’s 818,000 square feet</a>.</p><p>Other retailers followed. In 2021, Gap closed its three-level flagship, along with Express and Uniqlo, and in 2023, a gaggle of wireless carriers, like Verizon and T-Mobile, closed their flagship locations.</p><p>But signs of a recovery kicked off in 2024 when women's retailer Aritzia opened its store at 555 N. Michigan, taking over Gap's old space. When the Canadian company had announced in 2022 its plan for a 46,000-square-foot store, it was the largest lease on the Mag Mile in a decade and a turning point for the corridor, Bares said.</p><p>And with yoga brand Alo’s first Chicago store, 717 N. Michigan, already open by 2023, it seemingly re-energized interest among other retailers.</p><p>“Word got out that [Aritzia and Alo] were performing above expectation,” Kirsch said. “More retailers paid attention to the avenue. The more that they learned, the more they wanted to be a part of it.”</p><p>Retailers that left the Mag Mile, like Uniqlo, returned. Others, such as The North Face, relocated and often downsized, looking for a more desirable place on the street. And international brands, including Intimissimi, Mango, Falconeri and Charles Tyrwhitt, soon joined the bunch.</p><p>Italian cashmere label Falconeri said the Mag Mile was an ideal choice because it’s “one of the premier luxury shopping destinations” in the country, said Gianni Forlini, chief business officer of Oniverse U.S., which owns Falconeri and Intimissimi.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-140000" name="image-140000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/53177f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+423/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F97%2F7ce6a2484fac987c81982a6cbd20%2Fmagmile-261025-16.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1e7da20/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+423/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F97%2F7ce6a2484fac987c81982a6cbd20%2Fmagmile-261025-16.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/309487d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+423/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F97%2F7ce6a2484fac987c81982a6cbd20%2Fmagmile-261025-16.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of Falconeri at 630 N. Michigan Ave.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Michigan Avenue provides the visibility, prestige and customer base needed to introduce our timeless Italian cashmere and natural fiber collections to a broader audience,” he said in an email.</p><p>The store, which opened this summer, has been meeting the brand’s expectations, reinforcing its confidence in the city, Forlini said.</p><p>The corridor that was once full of legacy brands, like Banana Republic, Columbia Sportswear and Express, is now occupied by retailers popular with younger generations.</p><p>And it's also home to experiences like the Harry Potter Shop at 676 N. Michigan and the interactive gaming experience The Cube, 600 N. Michigan, as well as other concepts nearby such as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/04/17/mag-mile-upscale-magic-theater-tullman-hand-eye" target="_blank" ><u>The Hand & the Eye</u></a> magic theater, 100 E. Ontario St. — giving consumers an experience similar to malls. </p><p>“I want to say there's been six or seven really sizable deals, like massive deals,” Kirsch said. “Lululemon and Nike and the Candy Hall of Fame. Normally, a market like Michigan Avenue would get one of those per year, and we got three of them in 2026.”</p><p>The influx of new retailers has been satisfying for the real estate industry and the Magnificent Mile Associaton, after years of headlines about a downtrodden Michigan Avenue.</p><p>“People are waking up to great retail and leasing news,” Bares said. “But these deals have been years in the making, and that's part of the story that Michigan Avenue has been rebounding for the last, at least, two years.”</p>

entries.title: Obama Center values, respects its workers
entries.summary: <p>Barack and Michelle Obama chose the South Side of Chicago as the home for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/18/obama-presidential-center-opening-jackson-park" >Obama Presidential Center</a> in order to build an active and engaging campus for everyone, whether visitors live across the street or on the other side of the world.</p><p>Since June 19, we have seen that vision come to life in extraordinary ways. We have had the privilege of enthusiastically welcoming over 220,000 visitors to the presidential museum, and hundreds of thousands more have explored the remainder of the 19.3-acre center, free of charge. Thousands of local students have participated in field trips and after-school programming at the center. Families have gathered for picnics, barbecues, <a class="Link" href="https://www.obama.org/programs/presidential-center/" target="_blank" >Movies in the Park</a> and impromptu line dances. And on these same grounds, rising leaders from our global programs and extraordinary role models have assembled to discuss new ideas, bridge divides and build a brighter future.</p><p>Carrying out a mission of this scale requires tremendous effort, and our team works hard every day to ensure an exceptional experience for every visitor and program participant.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-210000" name="module-210000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Over the last 10 years, more than 4,500 workers have contributed to our mission, including those who helped design and construct this magical center, as well as those delivering programs that empower global change makers and improve the lives of boys and young men of color and adolescent girls. We are very grateful to them and proudly display their names on our <a class="Link" href="https://www.obama.org/press-releases/obama-foundation-announces-worker-appreciation-wall-honoring-nearly-4500-individuals/" target="_blank" >Worker Appreciation Wall</a> at the center, commemorating those who helped bring our vision to life.</p><p>Before we opened the center to the public, we partnered with four community-based organizations to identify and recruit local residents for approximately 200 front-line roles — our team members who would spend hours a day warmly engaging our visitors from around the world, answering an array of questions with a welcoming spirit and keeping our center clean and safe. Seventeen thousand people applied, and we hired tremendously talented individuals.</p><p>We knew these jobs would be demanding and wanted to give staff the tools and resources they need to perform at their very best. We worked with industry experts to help us build a robust staff training that is grounded in our values. In recognition of the caliber of employees we have working here, we designed a compensation and benefits package that is competitive and comparable to peer museums and cultural institutions across Chicago.</p><p>Understanding the tremendous work it takes to live up to our standards of excellence, our goal is to operate a workplace that treats all contributors with respect and where workers’ dignity is highly valued:</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-d4ee8631-cd9c-11f1-b60f-67d57bcffd5d" start="1"><li>We maintain a transparent, ongoing dialogue with our workforce regarding growth opportunities. We have been — and will continue to be — guided by the Obamas' values, competitive compensation rates and our financial condition each year when considering staff compensation and benefits. We just kicked off our 2027 budget process, which will be completed by year end. <br></li><li>Operating a world-class cultural institution year-round means our staffing needs have evolved from our pre-opening years, when operations were limited around the winter holidays. We needed to evolve in order to serve our community fully, because our magnificent campus is now open to the public year-round. <br></li><li>Since our opening in June, our employee turnover has been less than 10%, which is on par with peer organizations and which also includes planned departures as a result of the conclusion of the construction phase. </li></ol><p>As our staff begins to consider <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/07/obama-foundation-and-center-workers-unionize-open-letter-afscme" >union representation</a>, we will approach their right to make their own organizing decisions in good faith, with immense gratitude for their many contributions, deep respect for unions and a sincere commitment to working collaboratively with our partners in labor.</p><p>We are greater than the sum of our parts. The center tells a story that the extraordinary history of the Obamas wasn’t made by them alone; it was made by countless people upon whose shoulders they stand and those who have stood by them through all the ups and downs.</p><p>And so we take seriously our responsibility as fiscal stewards of the Obamas’ vision, so every dollar we invest must create lasting value for our visitors to the center and our amazing program participants for generations to come. We wouldn’t be able to achieve this vision without our talented and dedicated team.</p><p><i>Valerie Jarrett is CEO and a board member at the Obama Foundation.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Screening, support for people with dyslexia can transform their lives
entries.summary: <p>When my daughter was diagnosed with profound dyslexia in second grade, I didn't know where to turn. What saved us was luck: Her Naperville public school had an instructor certified in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wilsonlanguage.com/programs/wilson-reading-system/" target="_blank" >Wilson Reading System</a>, a literacy program designed for children and adults with dyslexia and other learning disabilities. My daughter was reading at grade level before she left elementary school. Her experience changed me as well. I left my corporate job, earned Wilson certification and enrolled in a postgraduate special education program. </p><p>Last month, my daughter began studying engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her outcome rested on a staffing coincidence. It shouldn't have. Dyslexia affects roughly <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33278155/" target="_blank" >1 in 5 people</a> in the United States. It's the most common learning disability and one of the most responsive to adequate teaching. Illinois now requires districts serving K-3 students to <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=1672&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=160580&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >report on early literacy screening</a>, which is progress. But screening is uneven, and too many schools lack the curriculum or trained staff to act on the results. We see the cost when adults in their 60s and 70s, screened for the first time, call our <a class="Link" href="https://educationaladvocacy-consulting.com/dyslexia-center/about-eac-dc/" target="_blank" >Educational Advocacy and Consulting Dyslexia Center</a>, relieved after a lifetime of believing they were not smart.</p><p>The instruction I give a second grader and a 65-year-old is remarkably similar: explicit, cumulative and multisensory. A high school student once called skywriting — tracing a word in the air while saying its letters — "ridiculous." Once I explained movement helps lock spelling, things clicked. A woman I worked with for five years had known about her dyslexia her whole life but never received instruction. Once she did, it was a game changer. She's since opened a business that's doubled in size.</p><p>During Dyslexia Awareness Month this October, I hope more people will get screened. A screening takes about 10 minutes and is often free or low-cost through nonprofits, university clinics, schools and centers like ours. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://dyslexiaida.org/" target="_blank" >The International Dyslexia Association</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.everyonereadingillinois.org/" target="_blank" >Everyone Reading Illinois</a> publish plain-language guides for those with dyslexia. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wilsonlanguage.com/" target="_blank" >Wilson Language Training</a>'s certified instructor directory shows who near you is trained in structured literacy.</p><p>If you're a parent, ask your children's educators if the district screens students for reading risks and if anyone on staff is certified in a structured literacy program. Many families are asking just this, which is why our therapists support 10 Illinois districts that don't have certified instructors.</p><p>My daughter learned to read because of luck. Every child in Illinois deserves better odds than that.</p><p><i>Cassie Clark, executive director, EAC Dyslexia Center, Naperville</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-350000" name="module-350000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>U. of C.'s failure to act has familiar ring</h3><p>I'm a proud graduate of the University of Chicago. My parents also attended, as did two of my children. I am profoundly disgusted by the university's current posture with respect to multiple reports of sexual assaults tied to U. of C. fraternities. The Sun-Times reported that the latest accuser just <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >filed lawsuit </a>but had reported the incident to the Chicago Police in February. The university claims it is just finding out about the incident, and pledges cooperation with the investigation after noting that it is not a defendant in the lawsuit. The alleged culprit was suspended by the frat, but apparently not by the school. It seems the university's position is that it is a hapless bystander since the fraternities are not official student organizations.</p><p>This reminds me of the legal state of play when cigarette smokers were suing the tobacco companies in the 1950s and '60s. The defendants avoided liability by claiming that their customers knew the risks as they continued to smoke and that the real culprit was asbestos, air pollution, etc. It wasn't until recently, with the benefit of internal scientific and marketing documents, Americans learned that the companies knew more, allowing imposition of massive liability. </p><p>What did and does the U. of C. (and other colleges and universities) know about what's going on in their fraternities? Have they tried to do a thorough assessment of the problem? How does it leverage the prominence of "Greek life" to boost applicant pools? Do donors who were fraternity members play a role in the schools' "What me, worry?" stance? What is the effect on its putative educational mission when multiple young ladies are lured into these gigantic mansions, slipped a mickey, assaulted in a locked bathroom and then face doxing and perhaps withdrawal from college? Surely there are legal theories under which institutional complicity in a long-standing pattern and practice like this could support liability.</p><p>I have no doubt that if the number of sexual assaults and the efficacy of universities response to them were a factor in the U.S. News & World Report's college rankings, the problem would be solved almost instantly.</p><p><i>Andrew S. Mine, Rogers Park</i> </p><h3>Close the door on racial profiling at bars, nightclubs</h3><p>With the return of college students to campuses, local bar and nightclub owners in the Chicago area look to get their fair share of the thriving $<a class="Link" href="https://www.statista.com/topics/1752/bars-and-nightclubs/" target="_blank" >37.6 billion industry</a>.</p><p>The problem arrives when thirst for profits inspires owners to discriminate against some customers instead of welcoming all patrons.</p><p>My <a class="Link" href=" https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1111/cico.12286" target="_blank" >research</a> as a sociologist on nightclub scenes in U.S. cities, including Chicago, show a frequent bias against Black patrons. Not everyone who can play gets to play.</p><p>How do nightclub owners make those choices?</p><p>Because appearance is key, nightclub owners often create dress codes that tell potential patrons what clothing is acceptable. Some nightclub dress codes, for example, list <a class="Link" href="https://www.barandclub.com/blog/nightlife/the-ultimate-guide-to-dress-code-for-nightlife-how-to-look-stylish-and-stay-comfortable" target="_blank" >smart casual clothing</a> — button-up shirts and casual pants for men and skirts and blouses for women. In principle, dress codes are fine. But in practice, they're problematic.</p><p>Nightclub staff do not enforce dress codes evenly. Access is based on race, ethnicity, presumption of socioeconomic status and other <a class="Link" href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/socf.12780" target="_blank" >factors</a>. So when Black patrons wear the same clothes as their white counterparts, they're often denied <a class="Link" href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/2332649217743772" target="_blank" >entry</a>.</p><p>My most recent study centered on Chicago shows more <a class="Link" href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/23780231251363299" target="_blank" >troubling news</a>. Not only did Black patrons continue to experience discrimination for nightclub access, but they also were being asked to pay higher prices for the same <a class="Link" href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23780231251363299" target="_blank" >alcoholic drinks</a> when they were allowed in.</p><p>Discrimination in nightclubs has gotten more complicated. But it is possible to shift these behaviors and exclusions if venue owners and their workers identify and eliminate impromptu actions and rules that can keep Black people from enjoying a night out.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://sociology.illinois.edu/directory/profile/rabm" target="_blank" ><i>Reuben A. Buford May,</i></a><i> professor and head, sociology department, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Public Voices fellow, the OpEd Project, and author, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/Urban-Nightlife-Entertaining-Culture-Public/dp/0813569389" target="_blank" ><i>“Urban Nightlife: Entertaining Race, Class, and Culture in Public Space”</i></a><i>.</i></p><h3>Switch to ACT creates more hurdles for Illinois students </h3><p>Illinois’ recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/07/06/sat-act-illinois-high-school-assessment-isbe" target="_blank" ><u>shift</u></a><u>,</u> replacing the SAT with the ACT as the state-mandated assessment tool, threatens high school students’ access to higher education. While vendor switches driven by state contract deals are common, the change introduces an extraordinarily burdensome series of steps students must take to signal their interest in a college. Taking the ACT is hard enough, but now students also are required to:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-9ec41541-cbf6-11f1-b28d-a70a2888f7a1" start="1"><li>Log into an online portal using a school-provided code.</li><li>Create an "optional" myACT account.</li><li>Select "Recruit Me" and enter parent contact information.</li><li>Trigger an automated parental consent request.</li><li>Await explicit parental approval before any score data or contact opt-in is released to colleges.</li></ol><p>This new process harms the very students who benefit most from colleges reaching out to them: first-generation applicants, students with limited access to college counseling and families less equipped to navigate an already complex process. </p><p>This barrier comes at a critical juncture for Illinois, which already faces a projected decline of nearly 20,000 college-going students by 2029 and an annual net loss of roughly 18,000 students who leave the state for college. Taxpayers fund in-school testing to broaden pathways for students, yet this workflow effectively cuts off in-state colleges from those very students.</p><p>Illinois and the ACT must immediately overhaul this process to establish meaningful, accessible choices for students rather than procedural hurdles that choke off opportunity.</p><p><i>Kent Barnds, executive vice president for strategy and innovation, Augustana College</i></p><h3>Pets don’t care which pronouns you use</h3><p>When I saw the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/10/21/wildlife-personal-pronouns-blagojevich-baar-topinka-trump-republicans-priest-crucifix" >headline</a> on Wednesday's Letters to the Editor page, I laughed out loud. I honestly thought it was going to be an ironic commentary about the obsession with pronouns that many people on the left have. It’s annoying enough that in recent years, we’ve been told to ignore common sense and hundreds of years of convention and use whatever pronoun someone prefers for himself, or herself, or “themself.” We must do that in order to not offend the person’s sensibilities or hurt his, her or their feelings in any way. If I happen to slip up and call a man “he” after he decided he wants to be called “they” or “them,” I’m considered to be insensitive and possibly transphobic or homophobic.</p><p>Now, apparently I also need to worry about not offending animals too, and address or refer to them using, “he, she, them or who.” If I slip up and refer to as animal as “it,” I must be some sort of animal hater.</p><p>I asked my male cat Sebastian how it felt about this. Its response was to curl up on my lap and watch the game with me while I stroked its neck and administered nightly treats. Then the purring began. Sebastian assured me that it doesn’t give a rat’s behind what pronoun I use, so long as the comfy couch, food, water and treats are all there.</p><p><i>Tom Miller, Orland Park</i></p><h3>Tax the bots</h3><p>I'm neither a foe nor a friend of Mayor Brandon Johnson. I am an advocate for humans in Chicago. To that end, I suggest that instead of taxing people, we should create a new tax for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/16/lawsuits-accuse-chicago-delivery-robot-companies-of-collecting-biometric-data" >delivery robots</a> and their "cousins" — self-driving cars (whenever autonomous vehicles are allowed to operate in Illinois.) That is where future growth is to be found: taxing increasing activities that detract from human community.</p><p><i>Andrew Davis, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>Design flaw </h3><p>Lee Bey's excellent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" >column</a> nailed it: Why repeat the same mistake that was made when Soldier Field had a humongous hot tub dropped into it? The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry doesn't need a welcome hall that looks more like a suburban shopping mall. What's next, an Old Navy store?</p><p><i>Kenneth Marier, Lake View</i></p><h3>Halloween hiccup </h3><p>When we were 14 years old, my best friend Connie and I got a rude awakening while begging for treats on a chilly Halloween.</p><p>We knew we were older and bigger than the other children running up and down the sidewalks in search of an inviting house. But for us, it wasn't the lure of actually scoring some candy and other goodies. We were just happy fooling adults who opened their doors and greeted us like we were the cutest things they'd ever seen. The goodies were just the frosting on the cake so to speak, because some treats actually did have frosting.</p><p>But our charade came crashing to an end when a very stern man opened his door, noted that Connie and I were well over 5 feet tall and told us to scram. We were not kids, he said, adding that we were too old to be horning in on a night meant for younger children. With a slam of his door, our night of dubious frivolity was over.</p><p>Connie and I spent the next hour sitting on a curb eating candy, but also pondering the mysteries of life. Too young to drink coffee. Too young to smoke. Too young for beer. But too old to celebrate Halloween going door to door. Life can be complicated. And cruel.</p><p><i>Kathleen Melia, Niles</i></p><h3>Deal breaker</h3><p>A thought for all Americans: Would you want Donald Trump negotiating a deal for you?</p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: Share your memory of the night the Cubs won the 2016 World Series
entries.summary: <p>When first baseman Anthony Rizzo caught Kris Bryant's throw just before midnight on Nov. 2, 2016, Cubs fans experienced something that hadn't happened in 108 years: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/11/3/18323919/108-years-and-10-innings-later-it-s-over-cubs-win-world-series" >a World Series championship.</a></p><p>Rizzo pocketed the ball, and fans celebrated like never before — at the game in Cleveland and in Chicago on the streets, in bars and in their homes.</p><p>As the 10-year anniversary of that night approaches, we want to hear your memories. entries.title: Dear Abby: Disliked dad's daughter receives no condolences
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A friend's wife's elderly biological father was killed in a one-car auto accident recently. She had been estranged from him for as long as I can remember (more than 30 years?) and told me over the years how much she hated him. She adored her stepfather, who died a few years back.</p><p>My friend is now upset with me because I failed to send condolences to his wife following her father's death, despite the hateful feelings she had voiced about him. I certainly had reached out to her after the death of her stepfather, for whom she cared very much.</p><p>What is the rule of etiquette when a person loses a family member they hated? What would I even say? "Sorry for your loss"? It just seems that any sentiment would be fake. — <i>NOT INSENSITIVE IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT INSENSITIVE:</b> I agree with you. Explain to your friend that you didn't mean to slight his wife, but after hearing how much she disliked her biological father for so many years, you didn't think she needed consoling. Then, in a separate call, tell his wife that you are sorry if your lack of response was hurtful to her, because it was not your intention.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> What do you do about a co-worker who sends mixed signals to you? I am a woman about 72 years old, and he is about 20 years younger. I believe he's single or unattached. I lost my boyfriend 10 years ago to heart problems.</p><p>Over the past three to four years, this co-worker has made cute faces at me, winked, gotten physically close, followed me in the workplace for a moment, etc. We have offered to buy each other a beverage. He's a good person but acts odd! I think he's shy or has social anxiety. What do you think is the cause of this behavior? — <i>PUZZLED AT WORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR PUZZLED:</b> You say he "sends mixed signals," but you've listed only behaviors that show interest. Perhaps this gentleman is flirtatious by nature, or perhaps he's always socially awkward. What you know for certain is that he enjoys your company and seems to be looking for companionship. I say follow through on that drink offer, but try not to read too much into it. You have nothing to lose, but you may gain a good friend.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our daughter has been in a long-term relationship with the most wonderful young man. They live together, and their commitment is strong. They have supported each other through severe illness, loss of parents, employment layoffs, etc.</p><p>When in social situations, we are often at a loss how to properly introduce him. He's an important part of our family, and we are proud of him, but he is not our son-in-law, and he is much more than our daughter's boyfriend. Any suggestions? — <i>TERM OF ENDEARMENT IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR TERM:</b> It appears your daughter and this young man are lucky to have found each other. My suggestion is to ask him how he would like to be introduced, and follow his lead. You can't go wrong that way.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: What Chicago ghost story or urban legend did you grow up with? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers what Chicago ghost story or urban legend did you grow up with? Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Resurrection Mary, the Halloween graveyard ghost."<br><i>— Terry Mankus</i></p><p>"The little girl whose ghost people claim to see at Bachelor's Grove Cemetery. I went there during the day and didn't really see anything out of the ordinary. I drove past one night and saw four or five hooded individuals in long robes crossing the road from the cemetery walking back to their car. The only way I could describe them would be like monks. Who knows what kind of crazy things they were doing in there!"<br><i>— Leo Peech</i></p><p>"My mother told me about a satanic house on Army Trail Road by a bridge. In Bartlett? She was a Realtor and knew."<br><i>— Ted Huck</i></p><p>"I always heard about haunted apartments and hearing kids play or voices but never did see anything except one time where I'm sure I saw a witch floating on Broadway and Devon up north."<br><i>— Jacob Schumacher</i></p><p>"The devil baby of Hull House. entries.title: Bears get surge from Colston Loveland, Luther Burden at just the right time
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams was agitating to return from his hamstring injury, he talked up his pass-catching corps. He called them the best in the world — “BIW” for short — and said he planned on making them even better.</p><p>“I'm going to keep putting the ball up in the air, you keep making catches,” he told them. “Then from there, we'll keep growing.”</p><p>Receiver Luther Burden and tight end Colston Loveland took that to heart.</p><p>Loveland has 24 more receiving yards in the past two games than he did in the first five games of the season combined. Burden has 41 fewer receiving yards the past two games than he did the previous five. Both played their best game of the season in Thursday night’s 30-24 win against the Patriots, with Burden totaling a career-best 130 receiving yards and Loveland a career-high seven catches.</p><p>“When you throw for 300 yards, I think you end up having some guys stand out and feeling pretty good about their performances at the end,” coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>This is what the offense was supposed to look like after Johnson talked up both Burden and Loveland all offseason long. Williams never doubted it, saying the Bears wanted to get Burden the ball “as much as possible” and that it was “It's just a matter of when” Loveland took off. The latter took on extra meaning late Thursday, when fellow tight end Cole Kmet was lost for the season with a right knee injury.</p><p>“Things are just clicking and happen to be there,” said Loveland, who has a touchdown reception in each of the past two games.</p><p>Johnson was bothered by two Loveland drops against the Patriots, which he called uncharacteristic, but said his second-year tight end is getting open with regularity.</p><p>“We know what we're getting there,” Johnson said. “We've just got to continue to find opportunities for him.”</p><p>Johnson was impressed with Loveland’s blocking on Burden’s touchdown, too. On third-and-17 with 21 seconds left in the first half, Williams threw a screen to Burden, who charged fron the right slot into the end zone behind Loveland and receiver Kalif Raymond.</p><p>“Then the whole cavalry came, the whole O-line showed up, and it was like a wave carrying him through there,” Johnson said. “He saw a little crease and hit the jets.”</p><p>Asked what he saw in front of him, Burden smiled.</p><p>“I saw a whole lot of money,” he said. “It was great blocks by my teammates. Shoot, we needed them.”</p><p>When he reached the end zone, Burden knew exactly what he was going to do. He told a cousin earlier in the day he’d mimic Johnson’s version of the “Stanky Leg,” the dance the head coach did in the locker room after beating the Falcons — and eventually after winning Thursday, too.</p><p>“He's elite with the ball in his hands,” Johnson said. “It's just a matter of how we can get it to him. Certainly not at a level where we're predictable either. We don't want it to just be screens or underneath routes. He's got more to his game than that. He's got more speed than that, too.”</p><p>As a kid, Burden was so dangerous with the football in his hands that his friends called him “Touchdown Luther.” His new nickname is far more sinister.</p><p>“Problem Child,” Williams said.</p><p>With the ball in his hand, he’s a problem for the opposition. Through seven games, Burden has 250 yards after catch. That ranks third among all NFL players, though with the caveat that he’s played at least one more game than everyone else entering Sunday’s slate. Only seven other players have more than 200 yards after catch.</p><p>“When I get the ball, I’m gonna be a problem,” Burden said. “Especially with too much space. I might go the distance.”</p><p>He caught a 26-yard pass on the Bears’ first offensive play Thursday. Later in the first quarter, he had a career-long 58-yard catch. Burden finished with four catches for a career-best 130 yards.</p><p>“The stuff you don’t think is gonna go to the crib, it just goes to the crib,” Burden said.</p><p>Bears coaches told Burden during the week that he had to be the engine of the offense, given how much his teammates feed off his energy.</p><p>“The passion I bring to the game,” he said. “The energy, the will, the want-to, the fire.”</p><p>Combine that with Loveland’s breakout, and the Bears have reason to be excited about their final 10 games of the regular season.</p><p>“I think we're kind of hitting our stride now, in terms of how we can game-plan this thing to where every guy is getting their fair share of touches,” Johnson said.<br></p>
