entries.title: Must the Bears — as lucky as they are good — always dance with danger?
entries.summary:
Three things I think I know about the Bears, who are in a sweet, 11-day break between games during which they can nurse various bruises, catch up on errands, ponder existential issues, call their mothers and throw things at the TV while watching their division rivals:

1. They are good and lucky: The Bears are 5-2 after holding on to beat the Patriots 30-24. Angels are singing. Heaven is ringing. Cats are purring. Contented fans still are licking au jus from their fake mustaches.

But does everybody realize how wildly different the tone and feeling toward this team could have been?

Imagine an alternate world in which (a) the completely unnecessary, bungled second-quarter handoff to offensive lineman Joe Thuney, (b) the absurd defensive breakdown on the Patriots’ 48-yard touchdown on the last play of the first half and (c) the very bad, late-fourth-quarter sack taken by quarterback Caleb Williams had led to (d) a missed Cairo Santos kick on a career-long 58-yard attempt and (e) the Patriots driving down the field and winning.

The Bears would be in last place in the division. There wouldn’t be enough hours in the day to criticize and complain.

This team really is good, but it almost seems to need danger in its life. The illegal forward handoff to Thuney — if Williams didn’t know the rule, his play-calling head coach must not have, either — came as the Bears were knifing toward the goal line like it was nothing. Instead, it snuffed out their momentum and they settled for a short field goal. This is not such a big deal; it’s fun for the whole team when self-indulgent calls are mixed in once in a while.

But these Bears scored 59 points in the opener and still had a win in doubt well into the second half, then came back in Week 2 and allowed only nine points but lost anyway. It’s still almost never easy for them. After all the slow starts necessitating comebacks last season, the 2026 Bears — better than they were last year on the whole, I think — won’t stop playing chicken.

2. They’ll miss tight end Cole Kmet: The best little thing about the Bears is how well and willfully their tight ends and wide receivers block, which, of course, isn’t a little thing at all. In fact, it’s one of the litmus tests of a team. No one took more pride in this area than Kmet, who’s out for the season after injuring his right knee. He helped create big holes, and his absence will leave one.

3. They’re still a playoff team: I know it’s true because I fumbled around online looking at various “simulators,” “probability tables” and the like and found every geek with tape on the bridge of his glasses is giving the Bears at least a 75% chance to get into the postseason dance. Then again, some of them also give the Vikings a healthy shot to win the Super Bowl, and we know that’s not happening.

Caleb-o-meter: 9 out of 10

He has improved by leaps and bounds from last season and put that on display the last two weeks, and just wait until he fully redeploys his legs. Look, you try running 21 mph.

Look who’s coming: the Seahawks

Don’t get too encouraged by the champs’ 3-3 record. They committed four turnovers against the 49ers and still lost by only three. They fell in overtime in Denver. They beat the Patriots with Drew Lock at quarterback. They have the top-ranked defense in the NFL. They’ll be more than a handful.

Fascinatingly, all the talk in Seattle at the moment is about whether or not coach Mike Macdonald should bench Super Bowl-winning QB Sam Darnold in favor of Lock, who played very well in the first two games of the season while Darnold was injured. In four games since getting back out there, Darnold has thrown seven interceptions and taken 13 sacks. OK, so you can be a little encouraged.

Take the North

Lions fan Cody DeLorenzo has averaged about three hours of sleep over the last week-plus, which doesn’t make things any easier when you’re amid a 313-mile run from Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin, to Ford Field in Detroit.

DeLorenzo, an ultramarathoner who says he runs 60 to 100 miles a week — “It’s just where I find peace,” he said — has been on a nine-day run to raise awareness for breast cancer while his wife, Shannon, is an active patient at the City of Hope treatment center in Zion. Both are 32.

Carrying a Lions game ball en route, DeLorenzo was scheduled to arrive at Ford Field in time for Sunday’s game against the Packers. Donations were being made at gameballrun.com as his run raised funds for the Game On Cancer initiative at Detroit’s Henry Ford Hospital.

“I’m really sore and really tired, slowing down. My legs are really beat up,” he told me Friday morning before pounding the pavement again, hoping to cover 70 more miles by the end of Saturday.

“I might be covering all the miles, but my wife is working her butt off. … She’s the strongest person I know.”

entries.title: Chatham landlord charged with sexually assaulting tenant and murdering another woman in same apartment
entries.summary: <p>A Chatham landlord was charged with allegedly sexually assaulting a tenant in the same apartment where he reportedly murdered another woman, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Jerry Powe, 58, was charged with first degree murder, aggravated sexual assault with a weapon and aggravated kidnapping, police said. </p><p>Police received a 911 call about 9:20 a.m. Thursday from a friend of a 28-year-old woman who reported being sexually assaulted at gunpoint by her landlord at an apartment in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/23/man-sexually-assaults-tenant-at-gunpoint-after-strangling-another-woman-in-same-chatham-apartment-police-say" target="_blank" >8100 block of South Ellis Avenue</a>, according to reports from the Chicago police and the city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communication.</p><p>The 28-year-old woman said while the attack happened, she noticed another woman who “may be dead” on a couch, according to the reports.</p><p>Around the same time, Powe walked into the Grand Crossing District police station and “admitted to killing victim by strangulation,” according to the police report. </p><p>When police conducted a well-being check at the Ellis Avenue address, they reported finding the door locked, and no one answering. Fire department crews opened the door and found the unresponsive victim, an unidentified 36-year-old woman, unclothed and covered in a sheet, on a couch in the living room, according to the report.</p><p>She was pronounced dead on the scene by the University of Chicago Medical Center, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office. </p><p>Powe was scheduled to appear in court Saturday. </p>

entries.title: It's time to give Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen his props
entries.summary: <p>Thirty-seven. Thirty-one. That’s it. So far.</p><p>It was the points the numbers represented that set off the contrast. Suspect from Day 1, the points put up by other teams against the Bears’ defense began to look and feel like anomalies.</p><p>Because, well, hell, on other days, in other games, where the numbers weren’t north of 30, the unit — whatever that happened to look like from week to week, whoever was able to suit up — defensive coordinator Dennis Allen put on the field to defend Chicago’s NFL honor somehow kept defying expectations.</p><p>It was recently said Allen had ‘‘arguably coached one of his best games’’ as the Bears’ DC. His blitz scheming called ‘‘brilliant.’’ His mastery to ‘‘manipulate the protection count,’’ as former NFL safety Matt Bowen referred to it, was ‘‘great football.’’</p><p>On the Patriots’ first drive Thursday night, in between downs, Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, maybe predicting whom their Amazon Prime team would have to give further accolades to after the game, side-barred a segment to give Allen his flowers. The word ‘‘genius’’ was being tossed around.</p><p>Before all of this, before these last few games in which the Bears’ defense — while in flux — still found an identity, before the season began, the responsibility that belonged to Allen was doubted at inception.</p><p>The rundown since: Holding three of the seven teams they’ve played to 12 points or fewer. Holding a running back who’s on the short list in the MVP conversation (Bijan Robinson) to nine carries was a thing of beautiful resistance and denial. A run defense last season that was 27th in the NFL sits at No. 8 so far this season. A third-down defense that ranks No. 2 in the NFL. A points per game and total yards given up that were, (dis)respectively, 23rd and 29th in the NFL last season are now categories in which the Bears’ defense stands eighth and 11th, respectively.</p><p>Holding a team in the Patriots, who had been averaging more than 32 points in their previous four games to 24. Their fewest since Week 2.</p><p>It’s all DA. Take away the 16 points the defense allowed the Falcons in the fourth quarter, the six-reception, 143-yard, two-TD peace de’ Christian Watson put on them a few weeks ago and the breakdown on the last play of the first half against the Patriots, and Allen’s ‘‘bend but don’t break’’ defense has been close to unbroken.</p><p>He lives in this Bears culture in some unique form of anonymity. Inside of the shadow coach Ben Johnson casts. Making lemonade outta Hennessy and bruised lemons. The Bears’ BKS.</p><p>No Montez Sweat, Tyrique Stevenson (though he played Thursday), Coby Bryant, T.J. Edwards, Dayo Odeyingbo. No prob. No panic. Daniel Hardy, James Lynch, Grady Jarrett, Cam Lewis, Clark Phillips, D’Marco Jackson. Risen to occasion and opportunity. Add the sustained glimpses of overachievement of rookies Dillon Thieneman at safety and Malik Muhammad at corner, and all Allen has to do is play perfect chess with the pieces he has to work with on any given week, at any given position.</p><p>The players he continues introducing to us are basically those with no names. A dubious defense to begin with, he has seen major members of his starting unit ‘‘Bear down’’ to both injury and suspension, yet has instilled a ‘‘next Bear up’’ mentality that in this seven-week run seems very 2012-14 ‘‘Thibs-ish.’’ He has lifted them from ‘‘no-names’’ to ‘‘know names.’’</p><p>As quarterback Caleb Williams’ return has shaped the way the Bears have looked since, so might the return of cornerback Kyler Gordon. Hidden. Go figure. The man about whom Allen said during his introductory news conference in 2025: ‘‘I have a vision of how we can utilize him.’’ To which Mark Grote on ‘‘Rahimi and Grote’’ said of Allen in direct relation to Gordon: ‘‘If Dennis Allen were able to get [Gordon] to double-digit sacks, he’d be the greatest [defensive] coordinator that ever lived.’’</p><p>Now out there, maybe, all things considered and implementable, Allen can do with and for Gordon what Johnson has done with and for Williams.</p><p>We’ll see.</p><p>As Williams said, ‘‘That’s who we are: We’re gonna keep score.’’ To apply thought to expectative theory and totally paraphrase what Linus said to Charlie Brown, ‘‘Keep the score low Dennis Allen. Keep the score low.’’</p><p>He has. For the most part. The perfect complement and contrast to Johnson’s mission in keeping the score high.</p><p>What’s going to haunt Allen is his defense allowing more yards per target to wide receivers than any defense in the NFL. Looking one way against the Packers, another way against the Falcons and yet another against the Patriots. There’s time to find themselves. Find consistency.</p><p>Again, we’ll see.</p><p>As we sit back, sippin’ on the Henn and juice he continues to serve us, we can, God willin’, trust the swerve of the Bears’ above-solid ‘‘D’’ is official and real. And if this newly expected run meets the expectations the city is carrying within about how attainable the pinnacle is, then Dennis Allen is quietly putting himself in position to be this era’s Buddy Ryan. In Chicago.</p><p>Not necessarily in stature or aura but in what every championship-chasing team needs the most: someone who, by hook or crook or any means, gets the improbable, implausible, unpredictable done.</p>

entries.title: On Angel Reese's manifesting and anti-manifesting
entries.summary: <p>While Angel Reese was watching the 2025 WNBA Finals from home, she texted her friend and former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> star Kahleah Copper to say: “Just give me one game in the playoffs.”</p><p>Lo and behold, she arrived a year later. After being traded to the Dream, Reese is now in the Finals MVP hunt.</p><p>A truly remarkable leap.</p><p>Reese credits her success to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/10/16/six-months-after-the-sky-traded-her-away-angel-reese-is-in-the-wnba-finals" >practice of manifesting</a>, what she calls speaking positively into her and her teammates’ lives. Interestingly enough, she also practices what I’ll call “anti-manifesting” — speaking misfortune into her opponents’ lives.</p><p>Just ask Valkyries rookie Aminata Gueye. With Valkyries starting center Kiah Stokes on the bench in Games 2 and 3, Gueye did her best against Reese. But Reese terrorized her, treating her presence as an invitation to drive, finish and flex.</p><p>“You can’t guard me,” Reese told Gueye, shaking her head and trotting back on defense. In more heated moments, Reese told Gueye that she can’t “f— with” her and that Gueye is a “bum a—.”</p><p>Observing Reese’s intimidation tactics can be momentarily unsettling. Gueye has played exactly seven games in her WNBA career and is not exactly the toughest foe.</p><p>But you have to remember that Reese anti-manifests everyone equally, regardless of pedigree. In the semifinals series, she did it to former MVP Jonquel Jones, telling her that she was too small and couldn’t guard her.</p><p>It’s part of the game for Reese, who says she intentionally tries to get in her opponents’ heads. After Reese notched her third straight double-double in Game 3 of the Finals, studio analyst and Dream co-owner Renee Montgomery asked Reese what’s going through her head when she gets down in a defensive stance, clapping in her opponent’s face.</p><p>Reese said she wants anybody she’s guarding to be “scared as s—.” Still, she acknowledged that not every part of her emotional range is calculated.</p><p>“I have my highs and my lows,” Reese said during the semifinals. “It will definitely get to a moment where I’m on my high, and then I come to the bench and be like: ‘[We need to] manage our emotions.’ And the team is looking like: ‘<i>You</i> saying that?’”</p><p>I like these little admissions from Reese in part because they quiet the debate about whether she is a hero or a villain. They bring Reese into focus as something more complex: a young, developing star who is influencing and being influenced by her teammates. They also reveal a self-awareness that, to a great coach, can be a strong foundation for growth.</p><p>***</p><p>The most common question I’m getting about Reese from longtime Sky fans, besides “How does she get her game-day blush to look so good?” is why the Sky couldn’t have gotten this version of her.</p><p>Did they fail to develop her into a Defensive Player of the Year and All-WNBA second-team player, or is she just benefiting from a better context in Atlanta?</p><p>I think it’s a little bit of both. To me, Reese has looked like the same player she’s always been. Which is to say, someone who improves every year and who thrives in big moments. Is anyone actually surprised that Reese is feasting on her first Finals experience, averaging 18 points and 12 rebounds on the biggest stage?</p><p>In Chicago, Reese never played in a playoff game. She never even made it through a full season without injury. Now she’s healthy, enjoying the fruits of Atlanta’s labor and adding to them on a team with an All-Star core the Dream spent years building.</p><p>One place the Sky clearly failed is her outside shooting. Dream coach Karl Smesko had a plan to get her to shoot it straighter, and Reese is now connecting on 44.1% of her three-point attempts in the playoffs. Meanwhile, Sky center and franchise pillar Kamilla Cardoso has attempted only two three-point shots in her career.</p><p>Not a good look for the Sky’s player development operation.</p><p>Reese’s departure and continued rise also don’t reflect well on their overall management. They traded up to draft Reese in 2024, which meant giving up the 2026 pick that became All-WNBA guard Olivia Miles. Then, after Reese broke out as an All-Star, they let her walk for two first-round draft picks in 2027 and 2028 that will likely come at the end of the round.</p><p>What I’ve argued all year long is that they shouldn’t have made such a big investment in someone they pitched as the face of the franchise without a rock-solid plan and the patience to see it through.</p><p>The fact that they fired Reese’s mentor Teresa Weatherspoon after one season in 2024, couldn’t repair the relationship when Reese publicly called out the team in 2025 and never developed her shooting range suggests the plan was flaky.</p><p>So flaky that the Sky should be feeling a little bit like Gueye right now: unnerved about how and whether they’re going to get back on track.</p><p>I worry that the Sky aren’t feeling this at all. The front office has said that they’re satisfied with the return they got in dealing Reese to Atlanta — that two first-round picks are significant — and that they don’t regret the draft capital given up to get her.</p><p>I’ve <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/09/24/the-first-step-to-a-busy-offseason-is-for-sky-principal-owner-michael-alter-to-own-up-to-mistakes" >said this before about the Sky</a>, and I’ll say it again: You can’t learn from something you don’t acknowledge as a mistake.</p>

entries.title: Offense puts on a show for No. 24 Wildcats vs. Rutgers
entries.summary: <p>Aidan Chiles threw for three touchdowns for the third time this season and rushed for two others to lead No. 24 Northwestern past Rutgers 42-14 on Saturday at Ryan Field in Evanston for a fourth straight victory.</p><p>Caleb Komolafe rushed for 150 yards and a TD, including a 56-yard dash. Griffin Wilde, who finished with 133 receiving yards, Alex Honig and Drew Wagner caught passes for scores as Northwestern (6-1, 3-1 Big Ten) raced to a 28-3 lead late in the first half.</p><p>Rutgers starting quarterback Dylan Lonergan left after sustaining a blow to the head 6 minutes, 25 seconds into the first quarter and didn’t return. He was initially replaced by AJ Surace, then by third-string QB Sean Ashenfelder late in the third quarter.</p><p>Antwan Raymond rushed for 150 yards on 18 carries and the lone Rutgers (2-5, 1-3 Big Ten) touchdown, a 46-yard run late in the third. The score was set up by the first interception thrown this season by Chiles, who finished with 219 passing yards and 83 rushing.</p><p>Rutgers' Dane Pizzaro kicked a pair of field goals.</p><p>Lonergan was replaced by Surace, who tossed for 64 yards but was sacked three times by Northwestern’s hard-nosed defense. The first sack led to a costly fumble that resulted in a pivotal Wildcats touchdown late in the first quarter that made it 21-3.</p><p>Ashenfelder was the victim of Northwestern's fourth sack of the day.</p><p>Lonergan was hurt when he scrambled up the middle for a 5-yard gain, then slid forward to the ground at the Rutgers 45 with two Northwestern defenders closing in. Lonergan’s momentum was finally stopped by Northwestern’s Kobie McKinzie as the two players’ helmets struck each other.</p><p>Lonergan remained down on the field for a couple of minutes, then was helped by staff to a medical tent.</p><p>Northwestern jumped out to a 21-3 lead after one quarter, then upped it to 28-6 at the half.</p><p>The Wildcats scored on the opening drive as Wilde caught Chiles' 13-yard TD pass 5:06 in. The 10-play series was keyed by Komolafe’s 30-yard run.</p><p>After Lonergan exited, Surace maneuvered the Scarlet Knights to field goal range. Pizzaro kicked a 43-yarder with 4:26 left in the quarter to cut it to 7-3.</p><p>Then the Wildcats raced down the field on only five plays to up it to 14-3, scoring on Chiles' keeper.</p><p>On the first play of Rutgers' next drive, Surace was sacked at the Rutgers 8 and fumbled with Northwestern’s Jamaal Johnson recovering. Chiles hit Honig with a 8-yard TD pass off the next snap to up it to 21-3.</p><p>Komolafe scored on a 33-yard run down the left side with 1:46 left in the half, capping a zippy 61-yard drive to increase the score to 28-3. Pizzaro booted a 35-yarder as time ran out in the half to make it 28-6.</p><p>A 43-year-run by Clay Thevenin, who finished with 166 yards on the ground, and 31-yard rush by Raymond moved Rutgers to the Wildcats 7. But Ashenfelder threw a pair of incomplete passes, then was sacked by McKinzie on a fourth-and-7.</p><p>Raymond rushed in with 8 seconds left in the third, and a two-point conversion cut it to 28-14.</p><p>Wagner pulled in Chiles' 4-yard toss in the end zone 4:28 into the fourth quarter for a 35-15 Northwestern lead. Chiles ran in his second TD, wide off a fake handoff, with 4:33 left to complete the scoring.</p><p><b>The Takeaway</b></p><p>Rutgers: The Scarlet Knights never really had a chance to get their offense rolling after Lonergan's quick exit. The severity of the QB's injury was not immediately known.</p><p>Northwestern: The Wildcats are technically bowl-eligible, but are going for much more. They're 6-1 for the first time since 2020 and the fourth time since 2000.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Rutgers: Hosts Michigan on Oct. 31.</p><p>Northwestern: Plays at Oregon on Oct. 31.</p>

entries.title: For Blackhawks to score, they need to shoot — it can be that simple
entries.summary: <p>The Blackhawks aren’t scoring enough. Part of the problem is they’re not shooting enough.</p><p>Sometimes it’s that simple.</p><p>“We can for sure shoot it more,” Connor Bedard said after practice Saturday. “What do we have, 20 a game? That’s not enough.”</p><p>Entering Saturday, the Hawks averaged 21.4 shots on goal per game, the second-lowest in the league. And while trying to rally in the third period of their 4-1 loss to the Canadiens on Friday, they mustered only four shots — none in the first 10 minutes.</p><p>Like Bedard said, not enough.</p><p>“I think there’s times where we can just throw it on net,” he said.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said as much Friday.</p><p>“My answer for [scoring droughts] will always be, you got to find a way to score dirty,” he said. “So we got to find a way to get more pucks around the cage.”</p><p>Generally, though, the Hawks look to maintain possession and get prime scoring chances. They’re not the Hurricanes, who look to shoot once they step on the ice. That philosophy did help them win the Stanley Cup last season, and they’ve picked up where they left off, ranking second with 33.5 shots on goal per game.</p><p>“We’re looking to make more plays, looking to get better chances,” Patrick Kane said. “Especially once you enter the offensive zone, you don’t want to give up possession by just getting rid of it and getting a shot on net. Sometimes you think there’s a better play and there’s not. There’s definitely times where you feel like you can shoot it a bit more.”</p><p>“If you’re at the blue line and there’s no one in front, there’s no point to shoot,” Bedard said. “But if you have guys in front, and for our [defensemen], we need to get in front of both of them so they feel comfortable shooting.”</p><p>Though Blashill is looking for that “dirty” goal to spark the Hawks — they’re averaging 2.2 goals per game, third-lowest in the league — he said he ultimately grades the team on scoring chances.</p><p>“Shots can dictate the way people see the game because it feels a certain way when you have a lot of shots compared to not a lot of shots,” he said. “The first step is having an attack mentality, meaning you look at the net first and whether that’s a shot or a play at the net. The second part of being able to get them through is shoot off the pass, so shooting quicker.</p><p>“Honestly, I can’t say we’ve passed up a lot of opportunities to shoot the puck. I can say we haven’t been in the [offensive] zone enough in general. As we grow as a team, we’ll be in that ‘O’ zone more. But I can say that’s been the biggest reason probably for the lack of shots.”</p><p>“You’re looking at ‘O’ zone time,” Andrew Mangiapane said. “You don’t want to waste a shot on net, they blow the whistle, they break the puck out, it’s in our zone now. It’s, let’s live to see another day, let’s rim it behind, let’s make a pass down low. Keeping the puck is better than a wasted shot on net sometimes.”</p><p>And other times — such as when a team isn’t scoring — it can help to just send the puck toward the net. What do hockey analysts always say? “Good things happen when you throw the puck at the net.”</p><p>“We’re going to try to create more quality,” Bedard said. “But we could shoot more.”</p><p><b>NOTES:</b> <b>Jeff Blashill</b> said left wing <b>Andrew Mangiapane</b> (lower-body injury) is good to go for the game Sunday against the Panthers. At practice, Mangiapane skated on the fourth line with right wing <b>Cole Smith</b> and center <b>Ryan Greene</b>.</p><p>• Defenseman <b>Bowen Byram</b> (upper body) participated in about half of practice, wearing a non-contact jersey. There’s no timeline for his return.</p>

entries.title: Eric Couper to Peter Panagiotopolous connection sets records, drives Notre Dame deeper into the 6A playoffs
entries.summary: <p>The quarterback-receiver chemistry driving Notre Dame’s high-powered offense began in a seventh-grade classroom at St. Juliana on the Northwest Side.</p><p>Peter Panagiotopolous and Eric Couper didn’t play football together then, but they became best friends. When Couper decided to switch from defensive player to quarterback when he started high school at Notre Dame, the two friends made it happen together.</p><p>“We just kept hitting random fields that entire summer before freshman year,” Panagiotopolous said. “We threw the ball around anywhere we could. That’s my best friend.”</p><p>Couper started as quarterback on the freshman team, but had to wait his turn before starting on varsity as a senior. Panagiotopolous caught just one pass his freshman year.</p><p>No one expected this duo to earn local headlines and set school records. But they have. Panagiotopolous is the school’s career leader in receiving yards (1,233) and receptions (85) and set single-season records this year in receptions (70), yards (1,015) and touchdowns (16). Couper set school season records for touchdowns (31) and passing yards (2,226).</p><p>“I can always trust [Panagiotopolous] to get open,” Couper said. “He’s not very tall, but he is fast, and he is smooth and will pretty much catch anything.”</p><p>Couper threw five touchdown passes, two to Panagiotopolous, in Notre Dame’s 44-0 win over Maine West in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class6a-illinois-2026" >Class 6A</a> opening round playoff game on Saturday in Niles.</p><p>“Eric is a major competitor and was right there with the two seniors that played last year,” Dons coach Dan DeFranza said. “So I knew he was going to play well this season, but the numbers have surprised me. I know he was very disappointed last year with that playing time. He is a real, real competitor.”</p><p>Couper was 9-for-11 for 207 yards against Maine West. Panagiotopolous caught three passes for 103 yards. Nathan Nowak, JD Look and Deonte Macon also caught touchdowns.</p><p>“Couper never played quarterback growing up, and Panagiotopolous had one catch freshman year,” DeFranza said. “These kids put in the work. They are really good friends, and they work hard together and put in the extra time together, and that shows.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Driver killed after dump truck overturns at Plainfield-area quarry
entries.summary: <p>A dump truck driver died Friday after the vehicle overturned at a rock quarry in unincorporated Plainfield, authorities said.</p><p>The Plainfield Fire Protection District was dispatched to the quarry at 22950 W. 119th St. about 4:08 p.m. Friday after receiving a report of an industrial accident, according to a news release.</p><p>Responders found the driver trapped inside the large overturned truck, and the driver was pronounced dead, fire officials said.</p><p>The Will County sheriff’s office and the Mine Safety and Health Administration are investigating.</p><p>The fire district said Saturday it had not yet been informed whether investigators had determined what caused the truck to overturn.</p>

entries.title: Even with first-time starter at QB, Illini knock off visiting Ducks
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Aidan Laughery ran for 123 yards and a touchdown and Collin Dixon made a diving catch for a 23-yard score late in the fourth quarter as Illinois defeated Oregon 21-10 on Saturday.</p><p>It was the Ducks’ first road loss in Big Ten play since they joined the conference in 2024. They had won 10 straight.</p><p>Michael Clayton II was 11-of-18 passing for 84 yards and two TDs for Illinois (4-3, 2-2), including the throw to Dixon in the corner of the end zone. Dixon had six catches for 65 yards.</p><p>“I have no idea how Collin made that catch,” Illinois coach Bret Bielema said about Dixon's game-clinching TD.</p><p>Dylan Raiola was 27-of-41 for 246 yards for Oregon (4-3, 2-2). Dakorien Moore caught nine passes for 70 yards. Jordon Davison had 14 carries for 92 yards and a TD and Dierre Hill Jr. had 83 yards rushing on 13 carries.</p><p>“Give credit to Illinois. They were the tougher team and that showed up in the second half," said Oregon coach Dan Lanning. “We have to evaluate who we are. Each person needs to look within and identify where they can improve.”</p><p>Illinois went in front for good at 14-10 early in the third quarter on a 9-yard play-action TD pass from Clayton to Christian Abney.</p><p>Laughery ran untouched 75 yards for a TD that trimmed the deficit to 10-7 with 2:15 to go in the half. Illinois had gained just 43 yards before Laughery’s score.</p><p>“I thought this team could do a lot better than what we've done,” Bielema said.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Oregon: Star quarterback Dante Moore was sidelined for a third consecutive game after suffering a concussion Sept. 26 vs. USC. The Ducks miss him. They've scored just 39 points in the games Moore has been out. The Ducks lead the nation in 30-plus points games (48) and TDs (312) since Lanning became coach in 2022.</p><p>Illinois: Clayton, a freshman, started at quarterback in place of fifth-year senior Katin Houser, who suffered a broken hand Oct. 10 vs. Michigan State. Clayton became only the sixth freshman in program history to start at QB, but he shared duties in the second half with Carson Boyd. Bielema called the rotation, orchestrated by offensive coordinator Barry Lunney Jr., “poetry in motion.”</p><p><b>Four Ducks down</b></p><p>Four of Oregon’s top wide receivers didn’t play. Evan Stewart, the Ducks’ leader with 27 catches for 352 yards and four TDs, had been suspended indefinitely following a DUI arrest early Sunday morning. Jalen Lott, Messiah Hampton and Jeremiah McClellan also missed the game due to injuries.</p><p><b>First misses</b></p><p>Oregon kicker Gage Hurych, the reigning Big Ten special teams player of the week after kicking three field goals in a win over Nebraska, missed two 52-yard attempts and a 39-yarder in the fourth quarter against the Illini. Hurych is 10 for 13 on field goals and 20 for 20 on PATs.</p><p><b>Up Next</b></p><p>Illinois: Plays next Saturday at Maryland.</p><p>Oregon: Hosts No. 24 Northwestern on Halloween.</p>

entries.title: Oswego East takes down Curie to win its first playoff game in 10 years
entries.summary: <p>Oswego East sophomore Carter Meindel has been thinking about this moment for a long time.</p><p>"I dreamed of this as a kid, coming to OE games, [being] on the sideline, watching," he said after quarterbacking the Wolves to a 49-8 win against Curie Saturday afternoon at Rockne Stadium in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" >Class 8A</a> opening round.</p><p>"It's been awesome to be a part of the [school's] first playoff win in 10 years."</p><p>Meindel completed 5 of 7 passes for 70 yards and one touchdown, a 32-yarder to Chase Lafin. Jeremiah Gbean ran for a score and the Wolves (5-5) had five more touchdowns on defense and special teams as they led 35-0 after one quarter and coasted home.</p><p>Jayden Andrews ran the second-half kickoff back 65 yards for a touchdown, Gavin Ortiz and Jack English ran punts back for scores, and Makane Tande recovered a fumble in the end zone.</p><p>Meindel and his teammates will get to play at least two postseason games this season thanks to the expansion of the playoff field from 256 to 384 teams. They play at Huntley (9-0) next week in the first round, and are glad to have the chance.</p><p>"I mean, it is what it is," Meindel said. "... It's a good opportunity for teams to show what they can do against good schools."</p><p>Senior tight end/linebacker Jack Ponto, who returned an interception 30 yards for a TD, agreed.</p><p>"You can't really control how the playoffs are," he said. "But we got this opportunity to play, so we're just taking full advantage of it."</p><p>The Wolves play in the Southwest Prairie West, which qualified all six teams for the expanded playoff field. Oswego East coach Tyson LeBlanc led Curie to the IHSA playoffs under the old system in all of his five seasons there before moving to his current team.</p><p>"The old-school purist in me feels you've got to earn the playoffs," he said. "But also, as a football coach and somebody who knows what the game of football can give to kids — one more opportunity to put the shoulder pads on isn't a bad thing."</p><p>It's especially important for a team as young as the Wolves. Meindel, one of five sophomore starters on offense, is in just his second season as a quarterback.</p><p>"I was a defensive guy up until last year," he said. "And one of our quarterbacks ... got hurt and I stepped up."</p><p>"[We're] asking a lot from him as a sophomore," Ponto said. "But every week he's been improving."</p><p>Still, Meindel knows there's plenty of room for growth.</p><p>"I feel like I need to stop turning the ball over as much, be a little safer with the ball," he said. "Otherwise I feel like I'm doing a pretty good job."</p><p>Harper Edwards caught four passes for 59 yards and a touchdown for Curie (5-5).</p><p>"We thought we would end the season a little better than we [did] this year," Condors coach Jarve Lewis-Bey said. "Even though we made the state playoffs and all that, it wasn't what we expected. We expected to play better."</p>

entries.title: 3 wounded in East Garfield Park shooting, one man in critical condition
entries.summary: <p>Three people were wounded in a shooting Saturday afternoon in East Garfield Park, including a man who was listed in critical condition, Chicago police said.</p><p>A 40-year-old woman and two men, ages 41 and 46, were standing near a corner in the 3000 block of West Flournoy Street about 2:49 p.m. when a vehicle approached and at least one person inside fired shots in their direction, according to police.</p><p>The woman was shot in the leg and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in fair condition. The 46-year-old man was shot in the buttocks and taken to Stroger Hospital in fair condition. The 41-year-old man was shot in the neck and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>Area Four detectives are investigating.</p>
